title: Jaito, 1923
hookLine: a long peaceful campaign over the deposition of the ruler of Nabha

cards: A continuous reading of the Guru Granth Sahib is under way. Readers take turns so the voice never stops, from the first page to the last. That unbroken reading is called an akhand path.
Then the police walk into the gurdwara, and the reader is taken away, mid-line. For the people sitting there, the question isn't politics anymore: a reading of the Guru has been cut off.
What happens next won't be over in a day, or in a season.

teach.b: Maharaja Ripudaman Singh of Nabha, a small Sikh state, was known for his sympathy with the Akali reformers. The British government forced him to give up his throne.
The Akalis took it as a blow aimed at the panth, and gathered to protest.
At Gurdwara Gangsar in the town of Jaito, in Nabha, Sikhs held an akhand path for the deposed ruler. The authorities stopped it and arrested those present.
Now the cause had a second side: the right to read the Guru Granth Sahib to the end.
Group after group set out for Jaito to begin the reading again, and group after group was arrested.
Histories of the movement record that one large jatha was fired on as it neared the town, and many were killed and wounded.
Still the jathas kept coming, peacefully, month after month, until the reading was finally allowed to go on.

teach.h: PATIENCE, THE BOW AND THE ARROW.
teach.b: In the saloks of Sheikh Farid kept in the Guru Granth Sahib, at Ang 1384, Farid says: make patience your bow, patience its string, and patience the arrow, and the Creator won't let you miss.
Jaito asked for that patience, not for a day but for seasons. It wasn't one brave moment. It was the same quiet choice, made again each morning, by people who knew where the road led.

how: Sikhs remember the Jaito morcha as one of the long peaceful campaigns of the gurdwara reform years; Gurdwara Gangsar at Jaito keeps its memory, and those killed on the way are honored as shaheeds.

games.q: your jatha's members ahead of you have been arrested on the road to Jaito. what do you do?
o: set out the next morning, peacefully, as planned.
give up; the road is closed.
games.why: group after group set out, peacefully, for months, until the reading at Jaito was allowed to go on.

practice: Let your breath settle into a pace you could keep all day, and count each breath out from one to ten, then begin again. When your mind wanders, don't scold it; just go back to one, the way a jatha set out again the next morning.
If you pray, say Waheguru instead of the numbers.

wordCard.voice: Jaito. The town in Nabha where an akhand path was cut off, and where jathas kept coming, peacefully, for months, until the reading could go on. Today's word.

orig.note: akhand path, an unbroken reading of the Guru Granth Sahib from beginning to end.

carryVoice: Your line: long and peaceful. Some answers take seasons, not days; the jathas kept walking anyway. Until tomorrow.
